_comment: Cambridge 0097's Thinking and Working Scientifically and Science in Context objectives for Stage 5, authored as reasoning prompts. These are the half of the coverage gap that needs no new topic: TWS and SIC are not subjects, they are how an investigation the unit ALREADY RUNS is framed - ask the question, pick the enquiry, name the risk, decide when to repeat, spot the anomaly, draw the conclusion, say who uses this science. Every prompt below is anchored to an investigation Grade 5 already has.
_vehicle: reasoningPrompts. The builder appends these to the named unit's own array, and shell/subjects/science.js renders it as 'Explain Your Thinking' - prompt, a textarea, the key ideas as a checklist, and the model answer behind a disclosure. It is MARKED: reasoningHits() checks the learner's text against keyIdeas and the section completes when every prompt is done. Checked before choosing it: complete() in course-app.js is add-only (`if (!wasDone) progress.completed.push(section)`) and nothing anywhere removes a section, so adding prompts cannot un-tick a section a learner has already finished. They appear as further work with the tick intact.
source: Authored 2026-09-17 against Cambridge 0097 Stage 5, anchored to the investigations in Grade 5 units 1-6. Not extracted from a book: the Teacher's Resource frames these for the teacher to deliver aloud, and this course has no teacher in the room.
_minimumCovered: One prompt per unclaimed Stage 5 TWS/SIC objective, plus three added 2026-09-18 for objectives that were cited but never actually asked of a learner: 5TWSm.01 (the particle model was taught as plain fact, never framed as a model with limits) and 5Ps.01/5Ps.03 (the sound concept added to Unit 4 was prose only - no exploration, quiz item or reasoning prompt ever asked a learner to investigate vibration, pitch or volume). Coverage is a number that only goes up.

prompts.prompt: You want to know whether bean seeds germinate faster in a warm place or a cool one. Write that as a scientific question, and say which kind of enquiry would answer it.
keyIdeas: A question you can actually test
A fair test, changing one thing only
Temperature is the thing you change
prompts.modelAnswer: The question is: does temperature change how quickly a bean seed germinates? A fair test answers it, because I can change the temperature and keep the water, the seeds and the soil the same. Simply watching seeds without changing anything would tell me what happens, but not what caused it.

prompts.prompt: You predicted that all ten beans in the warm jar would sprout. Eight sprouted. How accurate was your prediction, and what should you write about it?
keyIdeas: Mostly right, not exactly right
Say what the results actually showed
A prediction is not wrong for missing by a little
prompts.modelAnswer: The prediction was close but not exact. Eight of the ten sprouted, so warmth did help, which is the part I had right. I was wrong that every single seed would sprout - two did not, perhaps because they were old or damaged. A scientist says how near the prediction came rather than only 'right' or 'wrong'.

prompts.prompt: Your warm jar sprouted eight seeds and your cool jar sprouted two. Write a conclusion, and use what you know about seeds to explain why.
keyIdeas: State what the results show
Warmth speeds up germination
Link it to the seed waking up and using its food store
prompts.modelAnswer: I conclude that bean seeds germinate better in a warm place: eight sprouted in the warm jar against two in the cool one. That fits what we know about seeds. A seed needs water and a suitable temperature before it will wake up and start using its food store, and warmth makes that happen faster.

prompts.prompt: Your friend tested one seed in each jar and got one sprout and none. Why is your ten-seed test more trustworthy, and when should a measurement be repeated?
keyIdeas: One result could just be luck
More seeds, or repeating, evens out chance
Repeat when a result surprises you or two readings disagree
prompts.modelAnswer: One seed tells you almost nothing, because that single seed might have been a bad one. Using ten - or repeating the whole test - means one unlucky seed cannot decide the answer. Repeat a measurement when the result surprises you, or when two readings of the same thing do not agree.

prompts.prompt: You have four flowers: a hibiscus, a maize tassel, a grass flower and a mango blossom. Build a key of yes-or-no questions that would let a friend tell them apart.
keyIdeas: Questions with only two answers
Use only what you can SEE
Each question splits the group smaller
prompts.modelAnswer: Start with a question that splits the four in half, such as 'Does it have big colourful petals?' The hibiscus and mango blossom answer yes; the maize and grass answer no. Then split each pair again - 'Are the petals wider than your thumb?' separates hibiscus from mango blossom. A key works because every question has exactly two answers and each one cuts the group smaller.

prompts.prompt: You are going to open a flower and find the anthers and the stigma. Name the equipment you would choose, and say what each piece is for.
keyIdeas: A hand lens, to see small parts
Tweezers or a blunt pin, to separate parts
White paper or a tray, to lay them out
prompts.modelAnswer: A hand lens, because anthers and pollen grains are too small to see properly. Tweezers or a blunt pin, to lift the parts apart without crushing them. A sheet of white paper to lay each part on, so the pollen shows up and nothing gets lost. Choosing equipment means asking what the job needs, not taking everything on the shelf.

prompts.prompt: Before you take a flower apart, name two things you would do to work safely, and say why each one matters.
keyIdeas: Wash your hands afterwards
Keep anything sharp pointed away from fingers
Never taste any part of a plant
prompts.modelAnswer: Wash my hands when I have finished, because some plants irritate the skin and I do not want that in my eyes or mouth. Keep the pin pointed away from my fingers and away from the person beside me. And never taste any part of the flower - a fruit holds seeds and that does not make it food, and some plants are poisonous.

prompts.prompt: Who near you uses what you have learned about pollination in their work, and how do they use it?
keyIdeas: A farmer or fruit grower
A beekeeper
They use it to get more fruit, or more honey
prompts.modelAnswer: A farmer growing mangoes or tomatoes uses it: knowing that insects carry pollen from flower to flower, they avoid spraying while the trees are in flower, because killing the insects means less fruit. A beekeeper uses the same fact the other way round, placing hives beside a crop so the bees find nectar and the crop gets pollinated. Both are earning a living from one piece of science.

prompts.prompt: You are measuring how much water is left in a dish after a day in the sun. How do you make that measurement accurate?
keyIdeas: Use a measuring cylinder, not a guess
Read it with your eye level with the water
Read it the same way every time
prompts.modelAnswer: Pour the water into a measuring cylinder rather than guessing from the dish, because the cylinder has a scale. Stand it on a flat surface and read it with my eye level with the water, not from above - from above the number looks bigger than it is. And read it the same way every time, so that the readings can fairly be compared.

prompts.prompt: You are testing evaporation in three places: a sunny windowsill, a shady corner and a breezy doorway. Describe the table you would record your results in.
keyIdeas: A column for the thing you change
A column for the thing you measure
One row per place, with the unit in the heading
prompts.modelAnswer: Two columns at least: one for the place, which is the thing I change, and one for the water left in millilitres, which is the thing I measure. Three rows, one for each place. The unit goes in the column heading so it does not have to be written in every box. If I measure each place more than once, I add a column for each reading and one for the average.

prompts.prompt: Your three dishes lost 40 ml, 38 ml and 5 ml of water. Describe the pattern, and say what you make of the odd one.
keyIdeas: Two results are close, one is far off
The odd one is an anomalous result
Look for a reason - do not just cross it out
prompts.modelAnswer: Two dishes lost about the same, around 40 ml, and the third lost only 5 ml, which does not fit that pattern. That third reading is an anomalous result. I would look for a reason - perhaps it stood in the shade, or was covered, or I misread the scale - and say so in my write-up. An odd result is evidence about the method, not something to rub out.

prompts.prompt: You have the water lost from three different places. Which kind of chart shows it best, and what would a reader see at once?
keyIdeas: A bar chart, because the places are separate groups
One bar per place, height showing water lost
A line graph would be wrong - a line joins things that do not join
prompts.modelAnswer: A bar chart, because the three places are separate groups rather than one measurement changing over time. One bar per place, its height showing the water lost in millilitres. A reader sees at a glance which place lost most, and how big the difference is, without reading a single number. A line graph would be wrong here, because a line suggests the three places join up and they do not.

prompts.prompt: You have glass, greaseproof paper, card, a plastic bottle and a metal spoon. Sort them by how light passes through, and say how you decided.
keyIdeas: Three groups: transparent, translucent, opaque
Test each one - do not sort by what you expect
Hold it up to the light and try to see through
prompts.modelAnswer: Three groups. Transparent, where I can see clearly through - the glass and the plastic bottle. Translucent, where light gets through but shapes are blurred - the greaseproof paper. Opaque, where no light gets through at all - the card and the metal spoon. I decided by testing each one, holding it up and trying to read through it, rather than sorting them by what I expected.

prompts.prompt: Sorting materials into transparent, translucent and opaque is one kind of scientific enquiry. Name a different kind, and say how it is different.
keyIdeas: Sorting and classifying puts things into groups
A fair test changes one thing and measures the result
The question decides which enquiry to use
prompts.modelAnswer: Sorting and classifying is what I did: putting things into groups by a property I could observe. A fair test is different - there I change one thing on purpose and measure what happens, such as moving a torch further away and measuring the shadow. There are others too: observing over time, looking for patterns, and researching in books and other sources. The question you are asking decides which one fits.

prompts.prompt: You tested five materials once each by holding them up to a window. Suggest one improvement to the investigation, and explain why it would help.
keyIdeas: Use the same lamp at the same distance
Test each material more than once
Say WHY the change helps
prompts.modelAnswer: I would use the same lamp at the same distance instead of the window, because the daylight changed while I was working, and a cloud passing can make a transparent thing look translucent. Then the only thing changing is the material, which is the thing I am testing. I would also test each material twice, so that one careless look cannot decide its group.

prompts.prompt: You are going outside to measure a shadow every hour in the sun. Name two risks, and say how you would reduce each one.
keyIdeas: Never look straight at the Sun
Heat and sunburn
Reduce them with shade, a hat and water
prompts.modelAnswer: The first risk is looking up at the Sun to see where it is, which can damage your eyes - so I would look at the shadow instead and never up. The second is the heat: standing out every hour could burn my skin or make me dizzy, so I would wear a hat, drink water and wait in the shade between readings. Naming a risk first is what lets you plan around it.

prompts.prompt: How do people near you use the fact that shadows move in a pattern through the day?
keyIdeas: Shade for people, animals or crops
Knowing when a place will be sunny
Drying things in the sun
prompts.modelAnswer: People use it without calling it science. A market trader sets up where the building's shadow will fall in the afternoon, not where it fell in the morning. A farmer plants a shade tree on the side that will shade the animals at midday. Anyone drying maize or washing puts it where the sun will stay longest. All of that is using a pattern of shadows they have learned to predict.

prompts.prompt: People once believed the Sun travels around the Earth. Why did they think so, and what changed their minds?
keyIdeas: The evidence they had really did look that way
Better observation gave new evidence
Ideas change when the evidence changes
prompts.modelAnswer: It is what the sky looks like: the Sun rises on one side and sets on the other, every single day. With only your eyes, that is a sensible conclusion. What changed it was better evidence - telescopes, and careful records of where the planets appear night after night, which only make sense if the Earth is going round the Sun. Science changed its mind because the evidence changed, not because someone insisted.

prompts.prompt: A friend says the Moon must make its own light, because it shines at night. Use science to answer them.
keyIdeas: The Moon reflects the Sun's light
The phases are the evidence
Give the reason, not just the answer
prompts.modelAnswer: I would say the Moon has no light of its own; it reflects the Sun's. The evidence is its phases: if the Moon made its own light we would see the whole circle lit every night, but we see a different amount each night, because we are seeing how much of its sunlit half is turned towards us. That is using evidence to support the point, rather than just telling them they are wrong.

prompts.prompt: Satellites help farmers see where rain has fallen. Give one good effect and one bad effect of space technology.
keyIdeas: A good effect: better information, sooner
A bad effect: fuel burned, and debris left in orbit
Both sides are real at once
prompts.modelAnswer: A good effect is that a satellite can show where rain has fallen and where crops are failing, so help reaches the right district before people go hungry. A bad effect is that rockets burn enormous quantities of fuel, and worn-out satellites are left circling as debris that can strike the working ones. The same technology does both, which is why people argue about how much of it to build.

prompts.prompt: You want to know how long the Moon takes to go through all its phases, but you cannot watch for a month. Where would you look, and how would you decide what to trust?
keyIdeas: Secondary sources: books, encyclopaedias, an observatory's own pages
Check more than one and see whether they agree
Prefer a source that says where its facts came from
prompts.modelAnswer: I would use secondary sources - a science book, an encyclopaedia, or the pages of an observatory or space agency. I would check at least two, because if they agree the number is probably right, and if they disagree I know to keep looking. And I would trust a source that says where its information came from over one that simply states it.

prompts.prompt: The particle model pictures matter as tiny balls, packed tight in a solid and zooming apart in a gas. Name one thing that picture gets right about matter, and one thing it leaves out or gets wrong.
keyIdeas: Gets right: particles are packed close in solids and spread out in gases
Leaves out: real particles are not solid coloured balls, and forces hold them together
A model can be useful even though it is not exactly true
prompts.modelAnswer: The particle model gets the SPACING right: particles really are packed tightly in a solid and spread far apart in a gas, which explains why solids keep their shape and gases do not. What it leaves out is that real particles are not tiny hard balls with nothing between them - invisible forces hold them together, and they have no colour or fixed size the way a drawn ball does. A model is useful because it shows some real features clearly, even though you have to remember which parts are just for picturing it and which parts are actually true.

prompts.prompt: Stretch a rubber band between two fingers and pluck it. Plan a quick investigation: what would you look at and feel to find the SOURCE of the sound, and what do you predict you will find?
keyIdeas: Watch or feel the band while it is sounding
The band is moving quickly to and fro - vibrating
When the vibrating stops, the sound stops too
prompts.modelAnswer: I would pluck the band, watch it closely, and also touch it very lightly while it sounds. I predict I will see it blurring as it moves quickly to and fro, and feel it buzzing against my finger. The moment I grip the band still with my hand, the sound stops, which shows that the vibrating - not the plucking itself - is what was making the sound.

prompts.prompt: Using the same rubber band stretched between two fingers, plan two separate tests: one to make the sound LOUDER without changing its note, and one to make the note HIGHER without changing how loud it is.
keyIdeas: Pluck harder for louder, without changing the band's length or tightness
Stretch the band tighter, or shorten it, for a higher note
Loudness and pitch are changed by different things
prompts.modelAnswer: To make it louder, I pluck the band harder without changing anything else, which gives a bigger vibration and a louder sound at the same note. To make the note higher, I stretch the band tighter or press a finger partway along to shorten it, which makes it vibrate faster without changing how hard I pluck. Testing one change at a time is how I know loudness and pitch are controlled by different things.
